newsitem.title: USA: EPA to promote pollution trading to meet air goals.
newsitem.headline: EPA to promote pollution trading to meet air goals.

text.p: The Environmental Protection Agency plans to rely heavily on emissions trading programs to meet its tougher air quality standards for soot and smog, an agency official said on Wednesday.

"We believe that the cap-and-trade program works. We believe it is the best way to get results both for ozone precursors (smog) and, as far as we know, for fine particles (soot)," said EPA Assistant Administrator Mary Nichols.
The EPA is to release its plan later this month to meet the stiffer new standards that President Bill Clinton announced late last month.
The agency estimated it would cost roughly $6 billion to $8 billion a year in pollution controls to meet the new standards, which industry groups have blasted as overly expensive and unnecessary.

Nichols testified at a House-Senate Economic Committee hearing, where a committee report was released that praised the concept of trading credits to pollute as a way to cut costs of cleaning the environment.

The trading programs put economic value on allowances to pollute which give industries incentive to shift pollution reductions to plants that can make them at the lowest cost, so they can sell their excess credits.
A cap is placed on the overall allowed pollution, ensuring environmental improvements.

The Joint Economic Committee report said trading should have a bigger role in U.S. and international pollution control efforts, including the new domestic air standards and global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

It said the trading scheme for smog- and soot-forming emissions from stationary sources such as factories and power plants could be modeled on the system that has been used to curb sulfur dioxide emissions from power plants as part of the nation's effort to reduce acid rain.
Mobile sources of soot and smog -- cars, trucks and other vehicles -- could be regulated under a system that allows trading between diesel fuel and gasoline manufacturers, the report said.

Nichols said the EPA may need more authority from Congress to require states to participate in emissions trading programs, but she said most states recognize trading as the cheapest way to meet federal standards.
The panel's report also backed the administration's plan for an international trading program to carbon gases from burning fossil fuels that is warming the planet.

Potential costs of a sweeping initiative to deal with the many sources of carbon gases in countries with various levels of economic development "will almost dictate the adoption of techniques like tradable emissions, providing some flexibility in meeting reduction goals," the report said.
